newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Telstra dividend cuts, pushes back bond programme.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Telstra dividend cuts, pushes back bond programme.

text.p: The Telstra special dividend pushes back the prospective pattern of the federal government's bond programme over the coming year.
On a net basis, it cuts overall federal government bond issuance over the period by A$2 billion or more.

The federal government will now have an extra A$3 billion in cash in the middle of the year so it should have to borrow roughly that much less as it finances its operations and rolls over existing debt at that time.

But the transaction costs the government something less than A$1 billion in Telstra's sale proceeds that are supposed to be banked later this year, so it will have to raise more in bonds at that time.
Telstra said earlier today that it would borrow A$3 billion to pay a special dividend of that amount to the federal government, its 100-percent owner.
The transaction is supposed to be done in late June, so the government will be relatively flush with funds around the middle of the year.

Theoretically, that's A$3 billion that the government won't have to borrow at that time, but the actual impact is a little Treasury might decide to build up a little loose change for some reason, or its programme might be affected by such marketing issues as a desire to maintain liquidity in a particular line of stock.

An extra A$3 billion in debt must reduce Telstra's value to some extent. Analysts tell Reuters, however, that the loss of value will be less than A$3 billion, so the loss of proceeds will be less than A$1 billion.
Whatever the amount, the federal government will now have that much more to raise in bond sales late this year or early next.
SENATE NUMBERS
We were wrong.
Canberra Watch reported on Wednesday that Prime Minister John Howard's promise to neutralise senator Mal Colston's vote made no practical difference to Senate votes.
But there is a situation where it can make quite a lot of difference: amendments.

In short, the government can still get legislation through the Senate providing independent Brian Harradine votes for the bill, as before, but it cannot now prevent an amendment if Harradine joins the non-government parties.

Under the previous configuration of the senate, the government's position was quite strong. While it needed the support of both independents to pass some motion, it could vote down a motion with only one of them.
As noted on Wednesday, there are 37 government senators, 28 Labor, seven Democrats, two Greens and the independents Harradine and Colston. Total: 76.
A motion passes the Senate when more senators vote for it than against it. If the vote is tied, the motion is lost.
So in a 76-member senate, the government gets a motion passed with 39 senators, which is its own members plus the two independents.
To block someone else's motion, you only need 38, because a tie isn't good enough.

So, if Harradine had sided with all the non-government senators in seeking an amendment but Colston had stuck by the government, the vote would have been 38-all and the bill would have remained unamended.
But we will not be dealing with a 76-member Senate now if Colston votes with the government, because the prime minister promises that in that situation a government member will be voluntarily absent.
In a 75-member senate, the government wins with 38 votes, its own senators plus Harradine. This position is unchanged.
But the government now needs Harradine to defeat a motion, because if he votes with the non-government parties, they will have 38 votes to 37.
In theory, this has enormous implications, because a bill can be "amended" out of existence.
Harradine is unlikely to support such measures but he does from time to time seek more moderate amendments.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
